--- course-unit: ch09-agent-based-models status: complete --- # Agent-based models {#sec-agent-based-models} ::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"} **Workshop programme**: taught live on Day 3, Sessions 1 and 2. See the [full schedule](../workshop.qmd). ::: An agent-based model (ABM) represents a population as interacting individuals. The SIR labels remain familiar, but the model can now make explicit who contacts whom, when an agent changes status, and how an update schedule can affect results. This chapter uses a small, well-mixed ABM so that the connection to the population equations stays visible. ## Learning goals You will: - classify an individual-level SIR model and distinguish it from a count model; - implement a synchronous contact-and-recovery rule with Agents.jl 7; - collect model-level data with the current `StandardABM` and `run!` APIs; - name the pieces that define a neighbourhood in a spatial ABM, and say what changes when contacts are drawn from one; and - compare an ensemble of individual simulations with the deterministic SIR ODE while identifying effects that aggregation hides; - validate a model that has no reference solution to check against; and - judge when an individual-level model earns its *additional* cost over a population model, separately from whether a model needs to be stochastic. ## Model assumptions and classification Every agent-based model is built from the same three components [@datseris2022]: the **agents**, the individuals that act; the **environment**, the space they live in, which decides who is near whom; and the **rules**, what happens to one agent in one step and what happens to the world once per step. The sections below follow that order — `Person` is the agent, the `nothing` space is the environment, and `agent_step!` with `model_step!` are the rules — and the frame is worth holding onto, because the agents are usually the easy part while the environment and the rules are where the modelling assumptions live. The population has $N=1000$ named individuals. Initially 10 are infectious, 990 are susceptible, and none are recovered. At every $\Delta t=0.1$ time unit, a susceptible makes $K\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ random contacts. A contact chooses a uniformly random individual and transmits with probability $\beta$ if that individual is infectious. An infectious agent recovers with probability $1-\exp(-\gamma\Delta t)$. Recovered agents are immune. We use $c=10$, $\beta=0.05$, and $\gamma=0.25$. This is a **stochastic, discrete-time, discrete-state, individual-level** model. Time is discrete because `StandardABM` advances in integer steps; state is discrete because each `Person.status` is one of `:S`, `:I`, or `:R`. The population is well mixed because the model has no spatial structure: `StandardABM(Person)` uses the `nothing` space. This is an ABM even though its aggregated contact rule is designed to approximate mass action. ## Equations Let $Z_i(t)\in\{S,I,R\}$ be individual $i$'s status and $I_t=\sum_i\mathbf{1}(Z_i(t)=I)$. Write $p$ for the proportion infectious among the people a susceptible can actually *reach*. For a susceptible, the probability of no successful transmission in one step, conditional on $K_i=k$, is $$ \left(1-\beta p\right)^k. $$ Averaging over $K_i\sim\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ gives $$ \Pr(Z_i(t+\Delta t)=I\mid Z_i(t)=S) =1-\mathbb{E}\left[(1-\beta p)^{K_i}\right] =1-\exp\!\left[-c\Delta t\,\beta p\right]. $$ {#eq-abm-infection} The recovery probability is $$ \Pr(Z_i(t+\Delta t)=R\mid Z_i(t)=I)=1-\exp(-\gamma\Delta t). $$ The exponent in Equation @eq-abm-infection is a rate $\beta c\,p$ acting for a time $\Delta t$, and for small $\Delta t$ it is approximately $\beta c p\,\Delta t$. That matches the SIR force of infection $\beta cI/N$ exactly, **provided $p=I_t/N$** — which holds here only because a contact is a uniform draw from the whole population. That proviso is doing more work than it appears to, and it is the hinge for everything spatial later in the chapter. Nothing in the rules forces $p$ to be the global prevalence. Drawing contacts from a fixed neighbourhood instead makes $p$ the *local* prevalence among those few people, the two quantities decouple, and the resulting model is not a noisy version of the SIR equations but a different model that will not scatter around them. The individual model still carries more state than the population equations: each agent's current status is retained, so the population counts are a summary we choose to compute rather than the model's only representation. Contacts and potential transmission sources exist during an update but are not logged by this implementation; recording who infected whom would require an event history or extra agent fields. The ODE only tracks the totals and uses the deterministic flow $$ \dot S=-\beta cSI/N,\qquad \dot I=\beta cSI/N-\gamma I,\qquad \dot R=\gamma I. $$ ## Julia implementation Agents.jl 7 requires the `@agent` macro for supported agent types. In the installed 7.0.3 API, `NoSpaceAgent` contributes the mandatory `id` field; `StandardABM(Person; agent_step!, model_step!, properties, rng)` constructs a discrete-time model. We use a two-phase update: `agent_step!` reads the old statuses and writes `next_status`, then `model_step!` commits all changes. Without this separation, activation order could let a newly infected agent transmit in the same step. ::: {#code-ch06-setup .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} using Agents using CairoMakie using Distributions using OrdinaryDiffEq using Random using StableRNGs using Statistics const N = 1000 const I₀ = 10 const β = 0.05 const c = 10.0 const γ = 0.25 const Δt = 0.1 const nsteps = 300 const times = collect(0.0:Δt:(nsteps * Δt)) @agent struct Person(NoSpaceAgent) status::Symbol next_status::Symbol end ``` ::: `Person(NoSpaceAgent)` is not a class inheriting from a base class, and reading it that way causes trouble later. Julia keeps data in `struct` types and behaviour in functions, which are selected by the types of their arguments, so a struct has no methods of its own. What `@agent` does is copy in the fields the model machinery requires — `id` for a no-space agent, `id` and `pos` for a grid agent — and then add the fields you asked for. `Person` inherits no behaviour from `NoSpaceAgent`, because there is none to inherit; the rules arrive separately, as the ordinary functions below. The contact loop uses the model's random-number generator through `abmrng(model)`. `random_agent(model)` is the current Agents.jl helper for uniformly selecting an agent from a no-space model. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-rules .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function agent_step!(person, model) person.next_status = person.status if person.status == :S for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt)) contact = random_agent(model) if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β person.next_status = :I break end end elseif person.status == :I if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt) person.next_status = :R end end return nothing end function model_step!(model) for person in allagents(model) person.status = person.next_status end return nothing end susceptible_count(model) = count(person.status == :S for person in allagents(model)) infected_count(model) = count(person.status == :I for person in allagents(model)) recovered_count(model) = count(person.status == :R for person in allagents(model)) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-rules .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` recovered_count (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: The model properties are a named tuple, so `model.β`, `model.c`, and `model.Δt` are ordinary Julia field accesses. A named tuple cannot be written to, which is fine while every property is a constant of the run; a model that *updates* a property as it goes needs a `Dict` instead, as the awareness model later in this section does. The `mdata` functions below are called by `run!` at the initial state and after each step. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-constructor .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function initialize_model(seed) model = StandardABM( Person; agent_step!, model_step!, properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt), rng = StableRNG(seed), ) for id in 1:N status = id <= I₀ ? :I : :S add_agent!(Person(; id, status, next_status = status), model) end return model end model = initialize_model(20250711) agent_data, model_data = run!( model, nsteps; mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count], showprogress = false, ) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-constructor .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: `run!` returns two data frames: one for agent observations and one for model observations. We requested only model-level totals, which keeps the example small while retaining the full individual state inside the model. The first row is the initial condition because `init=true` is the default. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-ode .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} abm_states = Matrix(model_data[:, [ :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count, ]])' abm_times = Float64.(model_data.time) .* Δt function sir_drift!(du, u, p, t) β, c, γ, N = p infection = β * c * u[1] * u[2] / N du[1] = -infection du[2] = infection - γ * u[2] du[3] = γ * u[2] return nothing end ode_problem = ODEProblem( sir_drift!, [990.0, 10.0, 0.0], (0.0, nsteps * Δt), (β, c, γ, N), ) ode_solution = solve(ode_problem, Tsit5(); saveat = abm_times) ode_states = Array(ode_solution) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-ode .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 3×301 Matrix{Float64}: 990.0 989.499 988.986 988.46 … 247.327 246.6 245.886 10.0 10.2479 10.5017 10.7615 59.1809 58.4369 57.7002 0.0 0.253087 0.512444 0.77822 693.492 694.963 696.414 ``` ::: ::: The model time reported by a discrete `StandardABM` is the step number, so the explicit multiplication by $\Delta t$ maps it to the physical time used by the ODE. ::: {#cell-fig-ch06-abm .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (760, 430)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "time", ylabel = "people", title = "Well-mixed individual-based SIR") for (j, (name, color)) in enumerate(zip(["S", "I", "R"], [:steelblue, :firebrick, :seagreen])) stairs!(ax, abm_times, abm_states[j, :]; color, linewidth = 2, label = "$name (ABM)") lines!(ax, abm_times, ode_states[j, :]; color, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 1.5, label = "$name (ODE)") end axislegend(ax, position = :rt, nbanks = 2) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch06-abm .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` One individual-based SIR realization and the corresponding ODE trajectory. ::: ::: ### Space and neighbourhoods The model above has no space: `NoSpaceAgent` gives each person an `id` and nothing else, and `random_agent(model)` draws a contact uniformly from the whole population. Replacing that choice is the main way an ABM is extended, so it is worth naming the pieces. A **space** in Agents.jl is the structure that decides which agents are near which others [@datseris2022]. A model can define its own, and the library provides these: | Kind | Agents.jl type | Used for | |---|---|---| | Grid or lattice, 2D or $n$D | `GridSpace`, `GridSpaceSingle` | space as discrete cells | | Graph or network | `GraphSpace` | contact and social networks | | Continuous | `ContinuousSpace` | movement, flocking | | Street map | `OpenStreetMapSpace` | routes in a real city | `GridSpace` allows many agents per cell; `GridSpaceSingle` allows at most one, so filling every cell makes the grid and the population the same object. Whichever space is used, the property the rules actually consult is the **neighbourhood**: the set of agents within a given distance of a focal agent. Two model choices define it. The **radius** says how far to look, and the **metric** says how distance is counted. On a grid, `:chebyshev` counts a diagonal step as one step, so radius 1 gives the eight surrounding cells, the Moore neighbourhood; `:euclidean` measures straight-line distance and gives a disc; `:manhattan` sums the horizontal and vertical steps and gives a diamond. The shapes are the names, and only the Chebyshev count has a closed form you can do in your head, $(2r+1)^2-1$: | Metric | Shape | $r=1$ | $r=2$ | $r=3$ | |---|---|---|---|---| | `:chebyshev` | square | 8 | 24 | 48 | | `:euclidean` | disc | 4 | 12 | 28 | | `:manhattan` | diamond | 4 | 12 | 24 | A grid is also either **periodic**, wrapping at the edges so that every agent has the same number of neighbours, or **bounded**, in which case agents near an edge have fewer. A smaller neighbourhood is not automatically a lower risk, and under the rule used here it is a higher one: the number of contacts a susceptible makes is drawn from $\operatorname{Poisson}(c\Delta t)$ however many neighbours there are, so shrinking the pool leaves the contact rate untouched and raises the *proportion* infectious nearby, the $p$ of Equation @eq-abm-infection. A corner agent with one infectious neighbour out of three carries $8/3$ times the hazard of a middle agent with one out of eight, which makes the boundary the most dangerous place to live. That is frequency-dependent transmission — $c$ contacts per unit time whoever is available — carried over from the well-mixed model, and it is a choice rather than a property of grids. The alternative fixes the *per-neighbour* hazard: let each infectious neighbour transmit independently with probability $1-\exp(-\beta c\Delta t/n_0)$ for a reference neighbourhood size $n_0$, so the number of transmissions a susceptible receives is binomial in its infectious neighbour count. On a full neighbourhood the two rules are the same model, both giving $1-\exp(-\beta c p\,\Delta t)$ per step; at an edge the binomial rule scales risk down with the missing neighbours rather than up. What edges change under either rule is the number of *distinct* people reachable and the uniformity of the population: where an agent lives becomes part of the model, and the epidemic front can run out of room. Every grid model in this chapter wraps, which removes those effects and makes the two rules indistinguishable, so the Poisson contact loop carries over unchanged. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-space .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @agent struct GridPerson(GridAgent{2}) status::Symbol next_status::Symbol end demonstration = StandardABM( GridPerson, GridSpaceSingle((9, 9); periodic = false, metric = :chebyshev); model_step! = (model -> nothing), properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = Δt), rng = StableRNG(20250714), ) for position in positions(demonstration) add_agent!(position, demonstration; status = :S, next_status = :S) end centre_neighbours = length(collect(nearby_positions((5, 5), demonstration, 1))) corner_neighbours = length(collect(nearby_positions((1, 1), demonstration, 1))) (; centre_neighbours, corner_neighbours, at_radius_2 = length(collect(nearby_positions((5, 5), demonstration, 2)))) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-space .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (centre_neighbours = 8, corner_neighbours = 3, at_radius_2 = 24) ``` ::: ::: `GridSpaceSingle` holds at most one agent per cell, so filling every cell makes the grid and the population the same object. `GridAgent{2}` supplies `pos` alongside `id`, so a position field must not be added by hand. ::: {#cell-fig-ch06-neighbourhood .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} focal = demonstration[id_in_position((5, 5), demonstration)] ring1 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, demonstration, 1)) ring2 = Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(focal, demonstration, 2)) ring_color(p) = p.id == focal.id ? :black : p.id in ring1 ? :firebrick : p.id in ring2 ? :orange : :lightgrey fig, ax, _ = abmplot(demonstration; agent_color = ring_color, agent_marker = :rect, agent_size = 26, figure = (; size = (460, 460))) hidedecorations!(ax) fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch06-neighbourhood .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` A focal agent (black) with the cells within Chebyshev radius 1 (dark red) and the further cells added at radius 2 (orange), on a bounded nine-by-nine grid. ::: ::: Swapping `random_agent(model)` for `rand(abmrng(model), collect(nearby_agents(person, model, radius)))` turns the well-mixed model into a spatial one without changing anything else about the rules. That one line is the whole difference, so it is worth building the spatial model here and reusing it for the rest of the chapter. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-grid .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} @agent struct GridPerson(GridAgent{2}) status::Symbol next_status::Symbol end function grid_agent_step!(person, model) person.next_status = person.status if person.status == :S neighbours = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, model.radius)) for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt)) contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbours) if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < model.β person.next_status = :I break end end elseif person.status == :I if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt) person.next_status = :R end end return nothing end function initialize_grid_model(seed; infectives = I₀, radius = 2, timestep = Δt) model = StandardABM( GridPerson, GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev); agent_step! = grid_agent_step!, model_step!, properties = (β = β, c = c, γ = γ, Δt = timestep, radius = radius), rng = StableRNG(seed), ) for position in positions(model) add_agent!(position, model; status = :S, next_status = :S) end for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:infectives] model[id].status = :I model[id].next_status = :I end return model end ``` ::: {#code-ch06-grid .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` initialize_grid_model (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: A periodic $40\times25$ grid has 1000 cells, so filling every one gives the same $N=1000$ population as the well-mixed model, with every agent holding exactly 24 neighbours at radius 2 and no boundary special cases. `model_step!` and the three counting functions are reused unchanged: only the contact draw differs. Changing that draw changes the epidemic, and it changes it in a way the parameters alone do not reveal. The combination $\beta c/\gamma$ is the *mass-action* reproduction number, and on a lattice with a fixed neighbourhood it is not the model's $R_0$. Exercise 1 works out why. ### Behaviour that responds to information Every model so far has had people behave the same way from the first day of the epidemic to the last. Populations do not, and the rule below is the smallest departure worth making: **a susceptible who can see at least $m$ infectious people within `info_radius` cells takes precautions for that step**, and the chance of catching the infection from any one contact falls from $\beta$ to $\beta(1-\alpha)$. The information radius and the contact radius are separate numbers. One decides who you can *see*, the other who can *infect* you, and nothing forces them to match. Three settings let the same precautions be triggered by different information: `:none` is the model above, `:local` is the rule just stated, and `:national` reacts instead to the prevalence $I/N$ in the whole population, the way someone watching the news would. Note what the model grants that last rule — the true prevalence, at once and without under-reporting or delay. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-awareness .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function is_aware(person, model) if model.information == :none return false elseif model.information == :national return model.prevalence >= model.θ elseif model.information == :local return count(a -> a.status == :I, nearby_agents(person, model, model.info_radius)) >= model.m else throw(ArgumentError( "unknown information rule $(model.information); " * "expected :none, :local or :national")) end end function aware_agent_step!(person, model) person.next_status = person.status if person.status == :S transmission = is_aware(person, model) ? model.β * (1 - model.α) : model.β neighbours = collect(nearby_agents(person, model, model.radius)) for _ in 1:rand(abmrng(model), Poisson(model.c * model.Δt)) contact = rand(abmrng(model), neighbours) if contact.status == :I && rand(abmrng(model)) < transmission person.next_status = :I break end end elseif person.status == :I if rand(abmrng(model)) < 1 - exp(-model.γ * model.Δt) person.next_status = :R end end return nothing end function aware_model_step!(model) model.aware_days += model.Δt * count(p -> p.status == :S && is_aware(p, model), allagents(model)) for person in allagents(model) person.status = person.next_status end model.prevalence = infected_count(model) / N return nothing end ``` ::: {#code-ch06-awareness .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` aware_model_step! (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: `aware_model_step!` does two things besides committing the statuses. It adds up **aware person-days**, the number of susceptible people taking precautions times the length of the step, and it records the prevalence that the `:national` rule will read on the next step. The order of the three operations matters: `aware_agent_step!` decided this step's transmission from the statuses and the prevalence as they stood at the *start* of the step, so the count of aware people has to be taken before either is updated. Because `prevalence` and `aware_days` are written during the run, the properties are a `Dict` rather than the named tuple used above. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-awareness-model .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function initialize_aware_model(seed; information = :none, α = 0.5, m = 1, info_radius = 3, θ = 0.05, infectives = I₀, radius = 2, timestep = Δt) model = StandardABM( GridPerson, GridSpaceSingle((40, 25); periodic = true, metric = :chebyshev); agent_step! = aware_agent_step!, model_step! = aware_model_step!, properties = Dict( :β => β, :c => c, :γ => γ, :Δt => timestep, :radius => radius, :information => information, :α => α, :m => m, :info_radius => info_radius, :θ => θ, :prevalence => infectives / N, :aware_days => 0.0, ), rng = StableRNG(seed), ) for position in positions(model) add_agent!(position, model; status = :S, next_status = :S) end for id in shuffle(abmrng(model), collect(allids(model)))[1:infectives] model[id].status = :I model[id].next_status = :I end return model end function run_to_extinction(seed; max_steps = 10_000, kwargs...) model = initialize_aware_model(seed; kwargs...) steps = 0 while infected_count(model) > 0 steps += 1 steps > max_steps && error( "still infectious after $max_steps steps; a response too weak to " * "interrupt transmission can run far longer than these settings") step!(model, 1) end return (; final = recovered_count(model), aware_days = model.aware_days) end awareness_seeds = 7000 .+ (1:8) function summarise_awareness(; kwargs...) runs = [run_to_extinction(seed; kwargs...) for seed in awareness_seeds] return (; final = round(mean(r.final for r in runs); digits = 1), aware_days = round(Int, mean(r.aware_days for r in runs))) end ``` ::: {#code-ch06-awareness-model .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` summarise_awareness (generic function with 1 method) ``` ::: ::: Comparing the two information rules needs a fair basis, because either can be made to look better simply by having more people take precautions for longer. Aware person-days is that basis: it measures how much precaution was taken. The national threshold $\theta$ is therefore chosen so that the national rule has the population take roughly the same amount of precaution as the local rule does, and only then are the epidemics compared. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-awareness-comparison .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} awareness_comparison = ( nobody_reacts = summarise_awareness(information = :none), local_information = summarise_awareness(information = :local, m = 1, α = 0.5), national_information = summarise_awareness(information = :national, θ = 0.05, α = 0.5), ) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-awareness-comparison .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (nobody_reacts = (final = 656.0, aware_days = 0), local_information = (final = 47.1, aware_days = 4533), national_information = (final = 616.4, aware_days = 3946)) ``` ::: ::: At $\theta=0.05$ the national rule accumulates about 3,900 aware person-days against the local rule's 4,500, so the two populations take a comparable amount of precaution — the national one slightly less. The epidemics are not comparable at all: the local rule ends with roughly 47 infections and the national rule with over 600, against 656 when nobody reacts. Identical precautions, applied by a similar number of people for a similar length of time, and an order of magnitude between the outcomes. A large part of the explanation is targeting. Local information places precautions on people whose own neighbourhood holds a case, and on this grid every transmission happens between neighbours, so the precautions land where transmission is about to occur. A national trigger spreads the same effort evenly over a population that is mostly nowhere near a case, and switches it on only once prevalence is already high. This is a stripped-down, single-layer instance of a **coupled awareness–epidemic model**, in which a behaviour or awareness process runs alongside the disease process over the same individuals. The usual formulation gives each process its own layer of a multiplex network — a physical contact layer carrying the infection and a separate social layer carrying the information, with unaware–aware–unaware (UAU) dynamics on the second [@sun2024] — and richer versions let individuals weigh the cost and benefit of precautions as a game against their neighbours [@wang2025]. Our $\alpha$ is their awareness-induced protection factor written the other way round. Three assumptions make the result above an optimistic benchmark rather than a forecast, and each is a place the literature goes further: - **The information radius contains the contact radius.** With `info_radius = 3` against a contact radius of 2, at $m=1$ no susceptible with a current infectious contact-neighbour is ever missed. That containment is a mechanism built into the comparison, not an incidental parameter choice. In a multiplex formulation the two layers are genuinely different networks, which is what would be needed for a wider information radius to buy real advance warning. - **Awareness has no memory.** It is recomputed from scratch every step, so somebody who sees no infection this step behaves normally again. The standard treatment gives awareness its own forgetting rate, so vigilance decays rather than switching off [@sun2024], or lets the cost of compliance accumulate and fatigue [@wang2025]. - **Awareness is never transmitted.** People here only ever observe infection; nobody tells anybody. In the reference models awareness is itself contagious, spreading between neighbours at its own rate, so information and disease race each other [@sun2024]. Knowledge is also instantaneous and perfect, where real infection precedes symptoms and reporting takes days; both failures push the same way. And every aware person-day counts the same whether it stands for a mask or a closed shop, so it measures participation and is not a cost. One result from the wider literature is worth holding alongside ours: global, mass-media awareness lowers prevalence substantially when the protection it induces is near-complete, and does much less when that protection is only partial [@sun2024]. Local information is not simply better than national information in all settings. This rule is also the clearest answer to why the method is worth its cost. The national rule is a function of $I/N$, and a compartmental model can carry it as a transmission rate $\beta(I)$ that falls with prevalence, needing no individuals at all. The local rule is a function of one person's own neighbourhood. Writing it in $S$, $I$ and $R$ would require the number of susceptible–infectious neighbour pairs, then triples, and the system does not close. A model whose state is the three totals cannot express the rule. "Only an agent-based model can do this" would nonetheless be too strong. Pairwise formulations and message-passing methods reach the same class of rule, and the Markov-chain approximations used in both papers above yield an analytic epidemic threshold from the spectral radius of a matrix. They buy that tractability with either a restriction on the contact structure or a closure approximation, and what a closure discards is a local correlation — the Markov-chain treatments assume the states of neighbouring individuals are independent [@sun2024] — which is precisely what a rule like this one responds to. An ABM keeps the local configuration directly, and pays for it in computation. ## Validation The ABM has an exact bookkeeping invariant: every person has exactly one status. Consequently $S+I+R=N$ at every recorded step. The status graph is also one-way ($S\to I\to R$, with no return), so $S$ can never increase and $R$ can never decrease. Checking the recorded initial row as well confirms that `run!` collected the initial condition rather than the state after one step. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-validation .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} population_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(abm_states; dims = 1)) .- N)) @assert population_error == 0 @assert minimum(abm_states) >= 0 @assert abm_states[:, 1] == [N - I₀, I₀, 0] @assert all(diff(abm_states[1, :]) .<= 0) @assert all(diff(abm_states[3, :]) .>= 0) (; population_error, initial_counts = abm_states[:, 1], final_counts = abm_states[:, end], peak_abm = maximum(abm_states[2, :]), peak_ode = round(maximum(ode_states[2, :]); digits = 1), largest_gap = round(Int, maximum(abs.(abm_states[2, :] .- ode_states[2, :])))) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-validation .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (population_error = 0, initial_counts = [990, 10, 0], final_counts = [190, 63, 747], peak_abm = 188, peak_ode = 158.5, largest_gap = 31) ``` ::: ::: This realization peaks at 188 infectious where the ODE peaks at 158.5, about 19% higher and 0.9 days earlier, and the largest gap between the two curves is 31 individuals. One path is not the mean. To compare levels rather than a single random path, run a small ensemble of seeded replicates. The runs stay stochastic; the seeds only make them reproducible, and the model constructor gives each replicate its own random stream. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-ensemble .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function simulate_abm(seed) model = initialize_model(seed) _, data = run!( model, nsteps; mdata = [susceptible_count, infected_count, recovered_count], showprogress = false, ) return Matrix(data[:, [ :susceptible_count, :infected_count, :recovered_count, ]])' end abm_ensemble = cat((simulate_abm(4000 + k) for k in 1:16)...; dims = 3) abm_mean = dropdims(mean(abm_ensemble; dims = 3), dims = 3) infectious_rmse = sqrt(mean((abm_mean[2, :] .- ode_states[2, :]).^2)) @assert maximum(abs.(sum(abm_ensemble; dims = 1) .- N)) == 0 infectious_rmse ``` ::: {#code-ch06-ensemble .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 6.252915150099244 ``` ::: ::: The comparison is intentionally modest: 16 paths are enough to reveal the relationship and keep a teaching render quick, but not enough for a narrow confidence interval. The ensemble mean is not the same object as the ODE solution, and neither adjustment closes the gap on its own. At fixed $N$, adding replicates shrinks the Monte Carlo error but leaves the finite-population effects unchanged. As $\Delta t\to 0$ the frozen-step error vanishes and the stepped ABM converges to the continuous-time stochastic process for that same finite population. Its ensemble mean converges to that process's expected trajectory, which is generally not the ODE; recovering the ODE also requires a large-population limit. Individual epidemics take off at random times, so their peaks are spread over several time units. Averaging at fixed clock time therefore lowers the peak of the mean curve relative to the mean of the individual pathwise peaks: $$ \max_t \bar I(t) \le \overline{\max_t I(t)}. $$ That orders the two summaries, not the mean curve against every path: a replicate that fades out early can peak below the mean curve. Averaging is not interchangeable with taking a maximum, which Exercise 2 makes quantitative. ### Validating a model with no reference solution Everything checked so far leaned on the ODE. The spatial model cannot be checked that way, because the ODE is exactly the thing it moved away from: a gap between them is either a discovery about space or a bug in the contact rule, and the comparison cannot say which. This is the ordinary difficulty with an individual-level model, and it is worth having a method for. The method is to build a version of the model whose answer you already know. Keep every line of the rules, the same grid, the same population and the same parameters, and change exactly one thing: draw each contact from the whole population rather than from a neighbourhood. That model has no spatial structure left, so its $p$ is $I_t/N$ and it should reproduce the ODE to within the margins measured above. If it does, the code the two models share is behaving, and the search for an explanation of the gap narrows to the one line that differs. In this chapter that control is already built and already checked: it is the well-mixed model of the preceding sections, which differs from the grid model only in using `random_agent(model)` in place of `nearby_agents`, and whose ensemble mean was compared against the ODE above. A control that passes, though, provides less evidence than it appears to. It holds the shared code fixed and changes the contact draw, so it exercises the transmission rule, the recovery rule, the two-phase update and the Poisson contact count. It does **not** exercise the spatial machinery at all, because removing that machinery is precisely what it does. A wrong radius, a metric that is not the one you think, a grid that fails to wrap, or a neighbour set that includes the focal agent would every one of them pass this control and still be present in the spatial model. So check that machinery directly, on the grid the model actually runs on. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-probes .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} probe = initialize_grid_model(20250711) probe_neighbours = Dict(id => Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(probe[id], probe, 2)) for id in allids(probe)) @assert all(length(s) == 24 for s in values(probe_neighbours)) @assert all(length(Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(probe[id], probe, 1))) == 8 for id in allids(probe)) @assert all(!(id in s) for (id, s) in probe_neighbours) @assert all(id in probe_neighbours[other] for (id, s) in probe_neighbours for other in s) (; people = nagents(probe), cells = length(collect(positions(probe))), degree_at_radius_1 = length(Set(a.id for a in nearby_agents(probe[1], probe, 1))), degree_at_radius_2 = length(first(values(probe_neighbours)))) ``` ::: {#code-ch06-probes .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (people = 1000, cells = 1000, degree_at_radius_1 = 8, degree_at_radius_2 = 24) ``` ::: ::: Every agent has 24 distinct neighbours at radius 2 and 8 at radius 1, nobody is their own neighbour, and the neighbour relation is symmetric. A uniform degree is the effect of wrapping: on a bounded grid the first check would fail on every edge cell. Together the control and these four probes cover more than either does alone, and they still do not amount to a proof that the model is correct. ### Extinction and the shape of the outcome distribution Every run so far started from ten infectives spread across the population, and every one took off. Real outbreaks start with one case, and whether anything happens at all is then a matter of chance. That gives a second analytic result to check against: the branching-process argument of the jump-process chapter predicts that a single introduction fails to establish with probability $1/R_0$, which is $\gamma/(\beta c) = 0.5$ here. ::: {#cell-code-ch06-introductions .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} function grid_final_size(seed; radius, max_steps = 6000) model = initialize_grid_model(seed; infectives = 1, radius = radius) for _ in 1:max_steps infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model) step!(model, 1) end infected_count(model) == 0 && return recovered_count(model) error("epidemic still infectious after $max_steps steps") end introduction_seeds = 9000 .+ (1:200) final_sizes = Dict(radius => [grid_final_size(seed; radius) for seed in introduction_seeds] for radius in (1, 2)) fizzled = Dict(radius => final_sizes[radius] .< 100 for radius in (1, 2)) introduction_summary = [(; radius, neighbours = (2radius + 1)^2 - 1, fizzle_fraction = round(mean(fizzled[radius]); digits = 3), mean_if_it_takes_off = any(.!fizzled[radius]) ? round(mean(final_sizes[radius][.!fizzled[radius]]); digits = 1) : nothing, mean_over_all_runs = round(mean(final_sizes[radius]); digits = 1)) for radius in (1, 2)] ``` ::: {#code-ch06-introductions .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 2-element Vector{@NamedTuple{radius::Int64, neighbours::Int64, fizzle_fraction::Float64, mean_if_it_takes_off::Float64, mean_over_all_runs::Float64}}: (radius = 1, neighbours = 8, fizzle_fraction = 0.96, mean_if_it_takes_off = 128.5, mean_over_all_runs = 21.5) (radius = 2, neighbours = 24, fizzle_fraction = 0.555, mean_if_it_takes_off = 634.0, mean_over_all_runs = 285.0) ``` ::: ::: At radius 2 the fizzle fraction lands close to the mass-action $1/R_0 = 0.5$; at radius 1 it is nowhere near it, even though $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$ — and hence $\beta c/\gamma = 2$ — are identical in both. Changing only the size of the neighbourhood changes whether the branching-process prediction applies at all, which is the most direct measurement in this chapter of what the spatial structure is doing. ::: {#cell-fig-ch06-introductions .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} fig = Figure(size = (860, 360)) for (j, radius) in enumerate((1, 2)) ax = Axis(fig[1, j]; xlabel = "final number recovered", ylabel = "runs", title = "contact radius $radius") hist!(ax, Float64.(final_sizes[radius]); bins = 40, color = (:steelblue, 0.8)) vlines!(ax, [mean(final_sizes[radius])]; color = :firebrick, linestyle = :dash, linewidth = 2) end fig ``` ::: {#fig-ch06-introductions .cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` Final epidemic size across 200 introductions of a single infectious person, at contact radius 1 and radius 2. At radius 1 the outcomes form one continuous spread of small outbreaks; at radius 2 they fall into two separated groups, and the overall mean lies in the gap between them. ::: ::: The radius 2 panel is the reason to report two numbers rather than one. The outcomes are bimodal: most runs either die out almost immediately or grow large, and the mean over all runs falls in the sparsely populated gap between the two groups, describing an outcome the model almost never produces. The honest summary is a probability of take-off together with a size given take-off, because each of those describes something that actually happens. ## Interpretation and limitations The ABM can be extended by replacing the no-space model with a grid, network, or continuous space, or by adding age, behavior, vaccination, or household fields to `Person`. Those extensions change who can contact whom and can create clustering, superspreading, and spatial waves that a mass-action ODE cannot represent. The price is computational and inferential: agent rules need careful calibration, contact mechanisms can be difficult to observe, and random seeds do not remove structural uncertainty. That price is worth paying only for some questions, and two decisions that often get run together are worth separating. Whether a model should be **stochastic** is settled by whether counts are small enough that a probability is wanted rather than a curve — and the jump-process chapter answers that with no agents at all, more cheaply than anything here. Whether a model should be **individual and spatial** is a further question, and it is settled by whether contact structure or local heterogeneity moves the answer you were asked for. The single introductions above measure exactly that: identical $\beta$, $c$ and $\gamma$, and changing only the neighbourhood size moves the fraction of introductions that establish. Where such a shift does not occur, the equations are cheaper, faster, and easier to fit. Unlike the timestep of an ODE solver, $\Delta t$ here is part of the model rather than a numerical tolerance. In the ODE chapters the solver chose and refined it until it stopped mattering; in this model it sets how many contacts a person makes per step and how often anyone can recover, so it belongs to the model definition and has to be swept deliberately. Freezing the statuses within a step cuts both ways: an agent that recovers at the end of a step was treated as infectious for every contact attempt made during it, while an agent infected during the step cannot transmit until the step after. One of those raises transmission and the other lowers it, so the net direction is a question for measurement rather than argument, which is what Exercise 2 does. Contacts are drawn with replacement, which matters more on the grid than in the well-mixed model: a susceptible can meet the same neighbour twice out of only 24. That is not double counting, because $c$ is a rate of contact *events* rather than of distinct people met, and at $c=10$ with $\Delta t=0.1$ the mean number of draws per step is one, so a repeat arises in roughly 2% of steps. Drawing distinct people instead would make the number of contacts depend on how many neighbours a person happens to have, which is a different modelling assumption rather than a correction. Finally, a seed buys less reproducibility than it appears to. `StableRNG` fixes the random *stream*, not what the code draws from it: `shuffle`, Poisson sampling and `rand(rng, collection)` are library implementations, and any of them may consume a different number of values, or combine them differently, in another version. The figures quoted in this chapter therefore depend on the Julia version and the resolved package set as much as on the seeds, both of which are committed in this repository's `Project.toml` and `Manifest.toml`. On another combination, expect the conclusions to hold and the digits not to. Our synchronous two-phase update avoids an order artifact. The contact rule samples with replacement, so an agent can draw itself as a contact. A susceptible cannot infect itself, so that draw changes nothing, and keeping it in the pool is what makes the chance of drawing an infectious contact exactly $I_t/N$, the value used in Equation @eq-abm-infection. Excluding it would give $I_t/(N-1)$ instead. A network model would replace this convention with explicit contact constraints. The model is also discrete in time, so $\Delta t$ should be reduced and results checked for timestep sensitivity. Agents.jl's [agent definition documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/v7.0.3/agents/) and [data collection documentation](https://juliadynamics.github.io/Agents.jl/v7.0.3/data/) describe the v7 `@agent`, `StandardABM`, and `run!` APIs. The framework and its modeling rationale are described by Datseris, Vahdati, and DuBois [@datseris2022]. ## Exercises ### Exercise 1 {#ch09-ex1} Use `initialize_grid_model` from this chapter, which already supplies the periodic $40\times25$ `GridSpaceSingle` with `metric = :chebyshev`, one stationary agent per cell, and the same $\beta$, $c$, $\gamma$, and $\Delta t$. Run it at `radius = 1`, so that a susceptible can contact only the eight-cell Moore neighborhood, with the chapter's 10 initial infectives. Each run needs at least 60 time units, continued until $I=0$: spatial spread is far slower than well-mixed spread, and the 30 units used earlier in the chapter can end while both the well-mixed reference and the spatial realizations are still running, so a count recorded there need not be a final size. Confirm that $I=0$ at the end of every run before calling the recovered count a final size, and extend the horizon if necessary. Verify $S+I+R=N$, then compare the final size against the well-mixed model of this chapter over several seeds, using the same stopping rule. Explain which assumption behind Equation @eq-abm-infection has failed. Note that while $\beta$, $c$, and $\gamma$ are unchanged, the combination $\beta c/\gamma=2$ is the *mass-action* reproduction number and is not the spatial model's $R_0$; the substance of the exercise is to say why not, quantitatively — work out how many *distinct* susceptibles an index case reaches when repeated contacts land on a fixed pool of eight neighbors, and compare that with 2. Repeating the run at radius 5, where each agent has 120 neighbors, will let you check your explanation against a case where mass action should be much closer to recovered. ### Exercise 2 {#ch09-ex2} Run the ABM with $\Delta t=0.2$, $0.1$, and $0.05$, over the same physical time span in each case. For each value, report two different statistics of the infectious peak: 1. the peak of the ensemble-mean trajectory, $\max_t \bar I(t)$; and 2. the mean and standard deviation of the per-replicate peaks, $\overline{\max_t I(t)}$. Choose the stopping rule before you name either number a peak. At $t=30$ the epidemic is still going, with the ODE holding about 57.7 infectious, so a maximum recorded by then may well be the eventual peak, but nothing in the run so far establishes that: the path can still climb after the horizon ends, and so can the ensemble-mean curve. To report full-epidemic peaks, run every replicate for at least 30 time units and carry on until $I=0$. Cap the number of steps and raise an error if the cap is ever reached, so that a run which fails to finish is reported rather than cut short in silence. Replicates then stop at different times, so pad the finished trajectories with $I=0$ onto a common time grid before averaging them. If you stop at 30 instead, report both numbers as window maxima over $0\le t\le 30$ and name them that way, not as full-epidemic peaks. The deterministic ODE has $R_0=2$, $I_\text{peak}\approx158.5$ at $t\approx17.5$. Compare both statistics with that value, report whether each lies above or below it, and explain the differences you find. The inequality above orders the two stochastic summaries against each other; it says nothing about where either one sits relative to the ODE, so that has to come from your numbers. One part of each difference can be pinned down. Build the frozen-step mean-field map: apply the ABM's own per-step probabilities to deterministic mean-field counts, holding the infection probability at its start-of-step value for the whole step. This map is not the exact expectation of the ABM, so be careful about what it does and does not establish. The gap between its peak and the ODE peak isolates the frozen-step discrepancy, measured inside the mean-field approximation. The gap that remains between the ABM and the map holds everything else: the finite population, the spread of peak times across replicates, stochastic maximization (taking a maximum along a noisy path pulls the result upward), and whatever interactions those have with the timestep. Report a standard error for *both* estimates. These need different methods: the per-replicate peaks are independent draws, so their mean has the usual $\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{n}$ standard error, but the peak of the ensemble mean is a maximum taken over an averaged curve, and that same $\mathrm{sd}/\sqrt{n}$ formula does not apply to it. Resample whole replicate trajectories with replacement instead, and recompute the peak on each bootstrap sample. In an initial 64-replicate batch, the standard deviation of the per-replicate peaks was about 24 to 30 people across the three timesteps. With 16 replicates that is a standard error of roughly 6 to 7.5 people on a single mean. Comparing two timesteps is coarser still: the standard error of the difference is about 8.6 to 9.7 people for those same three standard deviations, which cannot settle a gap of a few people either way. Treat 16 as a quick exploratory minimum. To plan a longer run, work backwards from the half-width you are willing to accept. The number of independent replicates each timestep needs is roughly $$ n\approx 2\left(\frac{1.96\,\sigma}{h}\right)^2, $$ where $\sigma$ is the standard deviation of the per-replicate peaks and $h$ is the half-width you want for the approximate 95% confidence interval of the difference. The factor of two is there because both estimates carry error. The formula assumes the same number of replicates at each timestep and one $\sigma$ standing in for both, so it is a planning tool rather than an analysis of the runs you end up with. Taking $\sigma=30$ as a cautious planning value, $h=5$ people needs about 280 replicates per timestep and $h=2$ about 1730. Treat those two counts as starting estimates rather than fixed budgets. The value of $\sigma$ depends on the timestep and on the population size, so run a first batch, measure $\sigma$ from it, and put your own value back into the formula before committing to a long run. Reusing the same seeds across timesteps allows a paired comparison instead, which is cheaper only if the paired peak differences turn out to vary less than the peaks themselves. Two timesteps consume random numbers in different orders, so that correlation is not guaranteed. Measure the standard deviation of the paired differences on a first batch of runs and use it in place of $\sigma$ above, dropping the factor of two. That factor is not needed here because the paired differences already carry the variation from both simulations, so it would count it twice. ## Companion materials - [Slides](../slides/chapters/09-agent-based-models.html) - [Slides: awareness and behaviour](../slides/chapters/09-agent-based-models-awareness.html) - [Pluto preview](../notebook-exports/chapters/09-agent-based-models.html) - [Pluto source](../notebooks/chapters/09-agent-based-models.pluto.jl)
